inputs.need:
I am the physician lead for the regional central intake for adult gastroenterology referrals. About 9,400 referral letters a year arrive from 160 family practices as free-text letters or faxes; two triage nurses sort them and a gastroenterologist assigns urgency. Last quarter 22 percent of referrals were sent back to the family practice for missing information, most often a missing faecal immunochemical test result, missing blood results or no medication list, and the median time from receipt to a triage decision was nine working days. Family doctors complain that returned referrals disappear, and our triage nurses spend much of their day chasing information.

The region's digital health office is ready to switch on a structured electronic referral template with required fields for the six most common reasons for referral. Before we do, I want to redesign the whole triage process with lean methods: map the value stream from the moment a referral is written to the triage decision, find the waste, and use A3 problem solving with the nurses, two family doctors and the booking clerks. I want to know what published work says about structured referral templates and triage, whether they reduce returned referrals and triage time or just move the work to family practices, and how we should measure success without adding a burden to teams that are already stretched. We have no research money, but the region has given us a lean coach for three months.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; a lean coach for three months from January 2027; changes to the referral template go through the digital health office's monthly release schedule; triage nurse time cannot increase.

records.title: A structured electronic referral form for specialist outpatient referrals and the proportion of referrals returned for missing information
records.authors: Okwuosa-Brandt L, Hollis-Nakamura E, Sepulveda-Grant R
records.venue: Journal of Referral and Access Management
records.abstract: Two specialist services replaced free-text referral letters with an electronic form containing required fields for the most common referral reasons. We compared the 12 months before and after the change. Referrals returned to family practices for missing information fell from 19 percent to 7 percent, and the median time from receipt to a triage decision fell from 8 to 4 working days. The number of referrals received did not change. The comparison was uncontrolled, a new triage coordinator started in the same month, and the authors did not measure the time family practices spent completing the form.

records.title: Mandatory-field referral templates and triage time: a stepped introduction across 48 family practices
records.authors: Lindqvist-Adeyemi K, Carvalho-Stroud P, Mensah-Fairbairn A
records.abstract: A mandatory-field referral template was introduced to 48 family practices in four steps over eight months, in a random order of practice groups. Across 11,260 referrals there was no difference in the time from receipt to triage decision between periods with and without the template (adjusted difference 0.3 days, 95 percent CI -0.6 to 1.2). Returned referrals fell only in practices that used the template for more than half of their referrals. Overall, 38 percent of referrals bypassed the required fields by attaching a free-text letter. Practices reported that the template took longer to complete than a letter.

records.title: Tick boxes and workarounds: family physicians' views of structured specialist referral templates
records.abstract: We spoke with 24 family physicians and 11 practice staff in three regions about structured referral templates. Participants valued templates that pulled test results automatically and disliked required fields that repeated information already in the letter. Many described the templates as moving the specialist service's work into the practice without extra time. Several admitted attaching a letter to avoid required fields, especially for complex patients. Participants wanted to know what happened to returned referrals. The sample was drawn from practices that had volunteered for a regional template group.

records.title: Required faecal immunochemical test results in suspected lower gastrointestinal cancer referrals: an interrupted time series
records.venue: Journal of Referral and Access Management
records.abstract: A regional referral service made a faecal immunochemical test result a required field for urgent lower gastrointestinal referrals. In an interrupted time series over 30 months, the proportion of urgent referrals with a test result rose from 54 percent to 91 percent. Returned referrals rose in the first three months after the change and returned to the previous level by six months. Time to colonoscopy for urgent referrals did not change. Practices without access to rapid test kits returned the most referrals, and the authors warn that required fields can delay referrals from those practices.

records.title: Value stream mapping of a central referral intake: waste in handoffs and rework
records.abstract: A central referral intake serving six specialties mapped its value stream with nurses, clerks and referring practices. Staff spent about 60 percent of triage nurse time on rework: chasing missing information, re-keying faxed letters and answering practice queries about returned referrals. After a redesign that added a single returned-referral queue and a fixed daily triage time, the median lead time from receipt to triage fell from 12 to 6 working days over four months. No referral template was introduced. The evaluation was a before-after comparison without a control and without follow-up beyond four months.

records.title: Referral forms and guidelines for specialist referral: a systematic review of effects on referral quality and access
records.authors: Harcourt-Ibeh N, Tanaka-Poulsen R, Oduya-Ferris C, Kamara-Lind J
records.abstract: We included 21 studies of structured referral forms or referral guidelines for specialist outpatient services. Thirteen reported better referral quality, usually more complete information, with structured forms. Effects on waiting times were measured in seven studies and were inconsistent: three reported shorter times and four found no change. Only two studies measured the time family practices spent on referrals. Most studies were uncontrolled before-after comparisons, and definitions of referral quality varied. The authors conclude that structured forms improve completeness but that effects on access remain uncertain.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records from a second, broader search, appraised at abstract level; the first, narrow search for this intake's own question returned nothing and was confirmed empty by the investigator. Structured forms make referrals more complete (a review of 21 studies and a gastroenterology time series), but effects on access conflict: an uncontrolled before-after study reported triage time halving, while the best-controlled study, a stepped introduction across 48 practices, found no difference and widespread bypass of required fields. Family physicians describe templates as moving work into practices, and practices without rapid test kits return the most referrals. A value stream study shows that most triage nurse time is rework and that process redesign alone halved lead time. The body of evidence answers different questions with different designs, and no single certainty rating would be meaningful across completeness, triage time and practice workload.
response.gradeRationale: Not assessed as one rating: completeness, triage time and practice workload are separate outcomes, the only controlled study conflicts with the uncontrolled ones on triage time, and practice workload is barely measured. Per-record grades are given; overall certainty is left unassessed.
response.summary: Six retrieved records appraised; five claims recorded, one an inference with high uncertainty about conflicting results; overall certainty deliberately not assessed.

steps.note: Appraisal of the six retrieved records (S13). The records conflict on triage time; claim c3 is an inference over both conflicting records with uncertainty 'high'. The model declines one overall rating (explicit null on a model-owned field): issue 'cleared' at gradeOverall, and the stored certainty stays '' (not assessed), which holds at 875fe59 because nothing earlier was stored.

response.reading: Delay and returned referrals come from two sources: incomplete information at the practice and rework inside the intake. A template addresses the first and can worsen practice workload and bypass; process redesign addresses the second and halved lead time in one intake without any template. The evidence conflicts on whether templates shorten triage time (claim c3), so the redesign should treat the template as a countermeasure to test, with practice workload and bypass as balancing measures.

response.finer: Feasible with the lean coach and existing data; interesting to practices and the intake; novel in its combination; ethical as service improvement; relevant because the template goes live in 2027 either way.
response.summary: One time-bound improvement aim with a balancing limit.

response.rationale: The problem is a process with waste on both sides of the referral: missing information from practices and rework inside the intake. Lean methods (value stream mapping, A3 problem solving, standard work) fit a redesign led by the people who do the work, with the template as a countermeasure tested in sequence. Because the evidence conflicts on triage time (c1, c2, c3), the design measures it weekly rather than assuming it, and tracks practice workload and bypass (c4) and test-result completeness (c5).
alternatives: Switch on the template without redesign (refused: the controlled evidence shows no change in triage time and widespread bypass)
Stepped introduction of the template across practice groups with a formal comparison (refused: the region has one release schedule and no research resources; the aim is local improvement)
Model for Improvement with PDSA cycles (considered: similar measurement, but the intake's main problem is flow and rework, which value stream mapping addresses directly)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: A controlled comparison would answer whether templates work in general, which the region does not need to know; the intake needs to know whether its redesigned process improves, which weekly run charts can show.

decision.statement: Redesign referral triage with lean methods from January 2027, removing intake rework first and releasing the structured template as a tested countermeasure with a documented exception for unavailable tests, while measuring returned referrals, time to triage, template bypass and practice workload weekly.

response.overview: Lean redesign of the gastroenterology central intake from January to June 2027: a value stream map with nurses, clerks and two family doctors, then A3 cycles that first remove intake rework (a returned-referral queue and a fixed daily triage time) and then release the structured template with a documented exception when a rapid test is unavailable.
response.population: All adult gastroenterology referrals received by the central intake from 160 family practices; a twelve-week baseline from October to December 2026.
response.exposure: Returned-referral queue with a tracked status visible to practices; fixed daily triage time; structured template with required fields for the six most common referral reasons, released on the digital health office's monthly schedule.
response.procedures: Weeks 1 to 2: value stream mapping and A3 problem statement. From week 3: the returned-referral queue and fixed triage time. From the April 2027 release: the template. The intake extracts weekly counts from the referral system; a random sample of 20 referrals a week is reviewed for bypass (an attached letter instead of the required fields). Practice workload is sampled by asking five practices a month to time template completion.

outcomes.why: Practice workload is the main cost of templates (claim c4).

parsimony.simplestPath: One intake, one primary measure on a p-chart, countermeasures in sequence.

response.theoreticalFramework: Lean thinking: value stream mapping, A3 problem solving and standard work; no additional framework.
response.summary: Six-month lean redesign with returned referrals as the primary measure and bypass and practice time as balancing measures.

response.designSummary: Weekly time series: p-chart of returned referrals and run chart of median time to triage, with a twelve-week baseline and dated countermeasures.
response.sampleSize: The intake receives about 180 referrals a week. With a baseline of 22 percent, the p-chart's three-sigma limits sit about 9 percentage points either side of the centre line, so a sustained fall to 10 percent would show as a shift within a few weeks and single weeks below about 13 percent would signal special cause. Twelve baseline weeks give a stable centre line. The 20-referral weekly sample for bypass estimates a proportion of 25 percent with a 95 percent interval of about 19 points per week, so bypass is judged on four-week pooled samples.
response.primaryAnalysis: p-chart of weekly returned referrals with the baseline centre line and limits frozen after twelve weeks; shift, trend and point-outside-limits rules fixed before the redesign; limits recalculated only after a sustained shift.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Run chart of weekly median time to triage with the same rules; four-week pooled bypass proportions; descriptive practice timing; returned referrals by practice group.
response.missingData: Weeks with system outages are annotated and excluded from limit calculation, never imputed; missing bypass samples are recorded.
response.multiplicity: One primary measure; others are described with their charts and not tested.
response.software: Spreadsheet control chart template maintained with the lean coach.
overfittingGuards: Chart rules fixed before the redesign
Countermeasure dates marked before looking at the following weeks
No post hoc subgroup charts beyond the planned practice groups
response.summary: About 180 referrals a week make a p-chart sensitive to the targeted fall; bypass judged on pooled samples.

response.risks: Low for patients if no referral is lost; the main risk is that required fields delay urgent referrals from practices without rapid tests, which the documented exception addresses.
response.consent: No individual consent: the redesign changes a service process and uses aggregate counts; practices are informed before each change and can comment through the primary care network.
response.data: Weekly aggregate counts and a de-identified sample for bypass review; no patient identifiers leave the referral system.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: practices without rapid test kits, often rural or in deprived areas, returned the most referrals when a test field was required. Returned referrals are reported by practice group, the exception is monitored, and urgent referrals are never returned without a same-day call to the practice.
response.effectiveness: Success is fewer returned referrals and a shorter or unchanged time to triage without high bypass or practice burden.
response.efficiency: Uses the lean coach and existing staff; the template is already built.
response.costs: No new costs beyond staff time within existing roles.
response.grants: None needed; the write-up could support a regional application to spread the redesign to other specialties.
response.partnerships: Triage nurses, booking clerks, two family doctors, the digital health office and a patient partner from the regional patient advisory council.
response.rebPath: Service improvement using aggregate data; the regional quality office will be asked to confirm that no research ethics review is needed before publication, following the TCPS 2 guidance on quality improvement.
response.limitations: One intake, overlapping countermeasures, small practice timing sample.
response.summary: Low-risk service redesign with an urgent-referral safeguard and equity reporting by practice group.

steps.note: Reopen after ten of thirteen stages: the confirmed empty event, the second search and the unassessed certainty must all be kept; statuses are checked in the export.

response.title: Lean redesign of gastroenterology referral triage with a structured referral template: an improvement report from a regional central intake
response.abstract: Problem: 22 percent of gastroenterology referrals to a regional central intake were returned for missing information and the median time to triage was nine working days. Intervention: lean redesign of intake rework, then a structured referral template with a documented test exception. Measures: weekly returned referrals, time to triage, template bypass and practice completion time. Results and conclusions will be written after June 2027.
response.introduction: Structured referral forms improve completeness, but evidence on triage time conflicts and practice workload is rarely measured. No evaluation of a template introduced within a lean redesign of a central intake was found.
response.methods: Value stream mapping and A3 cycles from January 2027 after a twelve-week baseline; countermeasures introduced in sequence; p-chart and run charts with rules fixed in advance; SQUIRE 2.0 reporting.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the value stream map, the charts with dated countermeasures, bypass, practice timing and returned referrals by practice group.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret any change against the conflicting published results on triage time and state whether the template or the intake redesign accounts for it.
response.limitations: One intake; overlapping countermeasures; small practice timing sample; aggregate data only.
response.conclusion: To be written after June 2027; it will be limited to this intake and will not claim that templates shorten triage time in general.
response.summary: SQUIRE-structured draft with results left empty until data exist.
